settings.text: When your face goes red, how long does it take to come back down?
settings.a1_label: Under an hour, and it comes all the way down
settings.a2_label: Several hours, or the rest of the day
settings.a3_label: It doesn't fully come down any more

settings.text: In daylight, can you see fine visible threads on the cheeks or around the nose?
Does a product you used to tolerate now sting?
settings.a1_label: Often, and it starts within seconds

settings.text: Over the past year, has your list of triggers been getting longer?
settings.a1_label: Yes — things that were fine now aren't

settings.title: Some of both — which is the most common answer
settings.body:
Your answers point at a face doing two things at once: inflammation that shifts day to day, and vessels that may have started to hold open. That combination is the norm, not the exception.

It matters because the two halves need different things. The inflammatory half responds to a small, well-buffered routine held steady over weeks. The vascular half does not, and no serum will tell you otherwise.
settings.clinician_note: Worth having the visible vessels looked at before you spend money on topicals for them. That is a clinician conversation, and usually a light-based treatment one.
settings.cta_label: Read the five reasons a flush stops coming down
settings.link_label: Or start with what the barrier actually is →

settings.title: Barrier-led — your threshold has dropped
settings.body:
Stinging from products that used to be fine, a trigger list that keeps growing, redness that still comes back down: this is the pattern that responds to treatment.

It usually means the barrier has thinned, and a thinner barrier flushes at a lower threshold than it used to. Which is why the trigger list grows without anything new being introduced.

The move is subtraction before addition — shrink the routine, stop exfoliating, and hold one gentle, well-buffered active steady for eight weeks rather than eight days.
settings.cta_label: Read the five reasons a flush stops coming down
settings.link_label: Or read what we tell people to stop using →

settings.title: Mostly structural — and we want to be straight with you
settings.body:
Redness that no longer comes down, visible threads, and a trigger list that has stayed stable points more at the vessels themselves than at inflammation.

Once a vessel is structurally changed, no topical product closes it. Anyone telling you otherwise is selling. We would rather lose the sale than have you spend twelve weeks on the wrong thing.
settings.clinician_note: The honest next step here is a clinician, and usually light-based treatment — not a serum.
